T=test group C=control group; M=Male F=Female. 3.3. Risk of bias and quality assessment According to the instructions in the Cochrane Handbook of Systematic Reviews of Interventions ( Vavken et al., 2009 ) ( Figures 2 , 3 ), randomized controlled trials related to the risk of bias in seven aspects were evaluated. All the studies were randomized controlled trials. The generation of random sequences was either computer-generated or allocated and hidden using sealed envelopes. Among them, 3 literature adopted the random number table method, and 6 literature mentioned the software randomization method. Three literature did not clarify the random method. Regarding the concealment of the allocation scheme, two adopted the sealed envelope method, and the rest were unclear. One literature reported double-blinding of patients, researchers and evaluators, one reported blinding of subjects, and the remaining literature did not mention the blinding situation. Two literature mentioned cases of dropout. The causes of dropout were not related to the intervention effect and were determined to be of low risk. The summary and chart of the risk of bias assessment are shown in Figures 2 , 3 . FIGURE 2 Summary of bias risks. A risk of bias assessment chart for various studies from 2014 to 2025. Rows list studies, and columns show bias types: selection, performance, detection, attrition, reporting, and other biases. Green circles with plus signs indicate low risk, yellow circles with question marks indicate unclear risk, and red circles with minus signs indicate high risk. FIGURE 3 Risk of bias map. Bar chart evaluating risks of bias across different factors: random sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding of participants and personnel, blinding of outcome assessment, incomplete outcome data, selective reporting, and other bias. Each factor is assessed for low (green), unclear (yellow), and high (red) risk of bias. Most factors show a predominant unclear risk, with random sequence generation showing mixed risks. 3.4. Meta-analysis results 3.4.1. Pain score 3.4.1.1. Subgroup analysis based on the intervention measures of the control group Twelve studies reported pain scores, among which 11 used the VAS score scale and 1 used the NRS scale. A total of 705 patients were included. The smaller these pain score values are, the milder the pain degree of the patients will be. The heterogeneity among the studies was relatively large. The random effects model was selected to analyze the research data. The results showed that the pain score of the experimental group was significantly better than that of the control group, and the difference was statistically significant [MD = −1.32, 95% CI (−1.85, −0.79), I 2 = 93%, P < 0.00001]. Subgroup analysis was conducted according to the intervention measures of the control group. When the control group was treated with placebo, the results showed that the pain score of the experimental group was lower than that of the control group, and there was no statistically significant difference [MD = −2.32, 95% CI (−4.85, 0.21), I 2 = 85%, P = 0.07]; When the control group received other treatments, the results showed that the pain score of the experimental group was lower than that of the control group, and the results were statistically different [MD = −1.16, 95% CI (−1.69, −0.62), I 2 = 94%, P < 0.0001]. It indicates that extracorporeal shock wave can significantly improve pain compared with other treatment measures. As shown in Figure 4 . FIGURE 4 Forest map of subgroup analysis in the VAS control group. Forest plot showing mean differences between experimental and control groups across multiple studies, with confidence intervals. The plot includes subgroups labeled as "Sham group" and "Other group." Diamonds represent overall effects, and horizontal lines indicate heterogeneity. Heterogeneity statistics are provided, with chi-squared and tau-squared values, and a vertical line indicates no effect. 3.4.1.2. Subgroup analysis by evaluation period Twelve studies reported pain scores. A total of 705 patients were included. The smaller these pain score values are, the milder the pain degree of the patients will be. The heterogeneity among the studies was relatively large. Using the random effects model, the results showed that the pain score of the experimental group was significantly lower than that of the control group, and the difference was statistically significant [MD = −1.32, 95% CI (−1.85, −0.79), I 2 = 93%, P < 0.00001]. Subgroup analysis according to the assessment cycle showed that when the assessment cycle was >4 weeks, the results indicated that the pain score of the experimental group was lower than that of the control group, with no statistically significant difference [MD = −1.02, 95%CI (−2.50, 0.47), I 2 = 94%, P = 0.18]. When the evaluation period was ≤4 weeks, the results showed that the pain score of the experimental group was lower than that of the control group, and the difference was statistically significant [MD = −1.48, 95% CI (−2.09, −0.87), I 2 = 94%, P < 0.00001]. It indicates that extracorporeal shock wave can effectively alleviate pain symptoms in the short term, and the long-term pain relief gradually decreases. As shown in Figure 5 . FIGURE 5 Forest plot of VAS time subgroup analysis. Forest plot showing a meta-analysis of two subgroups, each comparing experimental versus control groups. The first subgroup (>4 weeks) includes studies with a subtotal mean difference of -1.02, with a heterogeneity I² of 94%. The second subgroup (≤4 weeks) shows a subtotal mean difference of -1.48, with I² of 94%. The total pooled mean difference across all studies is -1.32, with I² of 93%, indicating overall significant results favoring the experimental group. Confidence intervals are displayed graphically. 3.4.1.3. Perform subgroup analysis based on the type of shock wave A total of 12 studies were included, involving 705 participants. In the focused shock wave subgroup, the pooled average difference was not statistically significant (MD = −1.27, 95% CI: −4.08 to 1.53, P = 0.37), and there was a high degree of heterogeneity (I 2 = 93%). In the radiation shock wave subgroup, the experimental group showed statistically significant benefits (MD = −1.30, 95% CI: −1.84 to −0.75, P < 0.00001), although the heterogeneity was still high (I 2 = 94%). The overall pooled effect of all studies was statistically significant (MD = −1.32, 95% CI: −1.85 to −0.79, P < 0.00001), and the subgroup difference test indicated no significant differences among different shock wave types (P = 0.99, I 2 = 0%). As shown in Figure 6 . FIGURE 6 Perform subgroup analysis based on the type of shock wave. Forest plot showing a meta-analysis comparing experimental and control groups for focused and radial subgroups. The plot includes mean differences with 95% confidence intervals for each study. Subtotals for focused and radial categories are given, with overall effects illustrated by diamonds. Heterogeneity measures and test statistics are also provided, indicating statistical significance in both subgroups and overall. 3.4.2. QDASH score There were 5 literature that adopted the QDASH score in the study, and a total of 91 patients were included. The lower the QDASH score is, the better the recovery of the patient’s upper limb function is indicated. Heterogeneity analysis showed that there was significant heterogeneity among the studies. Therefore, a random effects model was adopted. The results indicated that the QDASH score of the experimental group was significantly higher than that of the control group, with no statistical difference [MD = −6.14, 95% CI (−14.00, 1.72), I 2 = 78%, P = 0.13), suggesting that extracorporeal shock wave had no significant improvement in upper limb function. As shown in Figure 7 . FIGURE 7 QDASH forest map. Forest plot showing mean differences for five studies comparing experimental and control groups. Mean differences range from -9.93 to 8.30 with a pooled overall effect of -6.14. The heterogeneity test shows a Tau squared of 58.26 and an I squared of 78%. The plot indicates no significant overall effect with a P value of 0.13. 3.4.3. Cooney score Five studies were included to evaluate the improvement of the Cooney score, with a total of 368 cases. The higher the Cooney score is, the better the wrist joint function of the patient will be. The heterogeneity among the studies was relatively large. A random effects model was used. The results showed that the Cooney score of the experimental group was significantly higher than that of the control group, with a statistically significant difference [MD = 13.84, 95% CI (5.04, 22.64), I 2 = 95%, P = 0.002]. It indicates that extracorporeal shock wave can significantly improve wrist joint dysfunction, as shown in Figure 8 . FIGURE 8 Cooney forest map. Forest plot showing a meta-analysis of five studies comparing experimental and control groups. Each study lists mean, standard deviation, total, weight, and mean difference with 95% confidence interval. Overall effect mean difference is 13.84, with a confidence interval of 5.04 to 22.64. The heterogeneity test shows Tau² = 95.05, Chi² = 87.65, degrees of freedom 4, with high heterogeneity (I² = 95%). The Z score for overall effect is 3.08 with p-value 0.002. The plot favors the experimental group. 3.4.4. Overall clinical effectiveness rate Six studies reported the clinical efficacy, involving a total of 434 patients. There was moderate heterogeneity among the studies. A fixed-effect model was used. The results showed that the clinical efficacy of the experimental group was better than that of the control group, with a statistically significant difference [OR = 5.44, 95% CI (2.99, 9.90), I 2 = 49%, P = 0.008]. The results show that compared with other measures, extracorporeal shock wave can significantly improve the clinical efficacy of stenosing tenosynovitis. As shown in Figure 9 . FIGURE 9 Clinical effects forest plot Forest plot showing odds ratios for six studies comparing experimental vs. control groups. Each study lists events, total, weight percentage, and confidence intervals. The central diamond represents overall effect with odds ratio of 5.44 (CI 2.99 to 9.90), favoring the experimental group. Heterogeneity: Chi² = 9.72, df = 5, P = 0.08, I² = 49 percent. Total events: 204 experimental, 155 control. 3.5. Multiple regression analysis Multiple regression analysis revealed that none of the examined variables—country, publication year, time period, intervening measures, or research setting quality—demonstrated a statistically significant association with the effect size. As shown in Table 3 . TABLE 3 The results of the multiple regression analysis. Covariates Comparision Coefficient Standard error t P Country 12 2.159 2.55 0.85 0.429 Publish 12 0.186 2.21 0.08 0.936 Period 12 −0.172 1.95 −0.09 0.932 IM 12 3.354 2.26 1.48 0.189 RSQ 12 4.914 3.64 1.35 0.225 IM=Intervening measure; RSQ=research on setting quality. 3.6. Sensitivity analysis Sensitivity analysis employing the leave-one-out method confirmed the stability of the pooled estimate. Sequential exclusion of individual studies yielded consistently negative 95% confidence intervals, supporting the robustness of the results. No single study significantly altered the magnitude or direction of the pooled effect. As shown in Figure 10 . FIGURE 10 Sensitivity analysis of pain conditions in two groups of patients with stenosing tenosynovitis. Forest plot showing meta-analysis estimates with individual studies omitted one by one. Each study from Karakuzu (2025) to Fu (2019) is plotted with confidence intervals. The x-axis ranges from -2.54 to -0.49. 3.7. Publication bias The Egger test and Begg test were used to assess the bias of the main outcome measure, pain results of tenosynovitis, in rotator cuff injuries. Both tests indicated the absence of significant bias (Egger test: P = 0.703; Begg test: P = 0.584). As shown in Figures 11 , 12 . FIGURE 11 Begg’s funnel plot with pseudo 95% confidence limits. Egger's publication bias plot showing a scatterplot with standardized effect on the y-axis and precision on the x-axis. Data points are distributed with a red regression line indicating potential bias. FIGURE 12 Egger’s publication bias plot. Begg's funnel plot shows the standard error of the standardized mean difference (SMD) on the x-axis and SMD values on the y-axis with yellow circles representing study data points. Pseudo 95% confidence limits are indicated by purple lines, and a horizontal red line marks the zero effect. 4. Discussion 4.1. Summary of main results This study is the first systematic review and meta-analysis based on randomized controlled trials (RCTS), aiming to explore the clinical effect of ESWT on stenosing tenosynovitis. The study focused on indicators such as the Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) for Pain or the Numerical Rating Scale (NRS), the score of the Upper Limb Dysfunction Questionnaire, the Cooney Wrist Joint Function Score, and the effective rate, and conducted an integrated analysis of the data of a total of 760 patients with stenosing tenosynovitis from 12 RCT studies. The subgroup analysis on pain relief results indicated that short-term pain relief was significant (p < 0.0001), while long-term effects gradually decreased (p = 0.18). This might be related to the short-term effect of extracorporeal shock waves. Additionally, when the control group used a placebo (p = 0.07), although there was no significant difference in the treatment effect of extracorporeal shock waves, this near-significant finding might suggest a potential therapeutic effect. Larger-scale and more effective studies might be able to confirm this result. Compared to the placebo, shock waves have a better pain relief effect than other drugs and physical therapies (p < 0.001). This might be due to the placebo effect, or the “instant stimulation” of shock wave therapy, which may trigger the activation of injury repair-related pathways and stimulate local inflammatory responses (therapeutic inflammation, which is beneficial for subsequent repair but temporarily aggravates pain perception), causing patients to perceive pain more significantly than the placebo group in the assessment of pain within a short period ( Li et al., 2022 ). The application of extracorporeal shockwave therapy (ESWT) demonstrated statistically significant and clinically meaningful improvements in both wrist joint functionality and overall therapeutic outcomes. In this Meta-analysis, although the Cooney score was positive, the QDASH score did not show significant improvement. This outcome might be due to the sensitivity and responsiveness. QuickDASH is a general upper limb function assessment scale, while the Cooney score is specifically for the wrist area. For the treatment of narrow tenosynovitis, the Cooney score has a higher sensitivity to changes in the condition. Minor but statistically significant changes in specific clinical indicators may not be captured by a broader functional assessment questionnaire covering the entire arm and shoulder. Although shock waves can promote tissue repair through mechanical stress, their improvement effect on structural changes such as thickening of the tendon sheath and tendon adhesion that have already formed is limited, and it is difficult to significantly improve the functional scores such as grasping and lifting of patients. Tendinosis of the flexor tendons, fibrotic thickening of the finger pulley, and tenosynovitis of the tendon sheath can be considered sonographic patterns with different responses to the shockwaves ( Kucera, 1977 ). Furthermore, the high heterogeneity of treatment parameters (energy density, number of shocks) and baseline characteristics of patients (disease duration, severity of the disease) in the included studies may further weaken the potential therapeutic effect. The results of this analysis indicate that for the treatment of stenosing tenosynovitis with the core goal of improving upper limb function, more high-quality studies are still needed to verify the effectiveness of shock wave therapy. Modern medical research shows that the etiology of stenosing tenosynovitis is related to chronic strain, mechanical compression, endocrine disorders, anatomical abnormalities, infectious factors and other factors ( Vuillemin et al., 2012 ). Repeated flexion and extension of fingers or wrists leading to excessive friction between tendons and tendon sheaths, long-term holding of hard objects causing local compression, endocrine changes caused by pregnancy or hypothyroidism, and anatomical factors such as congenital abnormal tendon course or tendon sheath stenosis may all induce this disease ( Ponomareva et al., 1979 ; Fakoya et al., 2023 ). Its pathogenesis is considered to be related to the inflammatory response of tendon sheath tissue, tendon degeneration, imbalance of synovial fluid secretion and biomechanical abnormalities ( Hittmair et al., 2012 ). Local inflammatory medium infiltration leads to thickening and fibrosis of the tendon sheath. Long-term compression of the tendon results in edema and deformation. The reduction of synovial fluid secretion intensifies friction. The abnormal force application pattern of the hand alters the biomechanical balance of the joint, which is a key link in the progression of the disease ( Cheng et al., 2013 ; Liu et al., 2022 ; Choi et al., 2025 ). This disease is more common among manual workers, middle-aged and elderly people, and postpartum women. Through conservative treatment (such as medication and physical therapy) or surgical intervention, the symptoms can be relieved. However, conservative treatment is prone to recurrence, surgery has the risks of trauma and complications, and currently there is a lack of specific treatment methods targeting the pathological mechanism ( Hittmair et al., 2012 ; Ferrara et al., 2020 ). Based on this, shock wave therapy has shown unique advantages and broad prospects in clinical applications due to its characteristics of non-invasiveness, strong targeting and few complications. In recent years, the clinical research and mechanism exploration of shock wave therapy for stenosing tenosynovitis have been increasingly in-depth and have received extensive attention in the field of rehabilitation medicine ( Malliaropoulos et al., 2016 ). A large number of clinical studies and basic experiments have confirmed that ESWT can not only effectively relieve pain and improve the function of the carpal and finger joints, but also exert therapeutic effects by regulating inflammatory responses and tissue repair mechanisms ( Auersperg and Trieb, 2020 ; Charles et al., 2023 ). Li et al. - By constructing a rat model of tenosynovitis, it was found that shock wave therapy could activate the PI3K/Akt signaling pathway, promote the proliferation of fibroblasts and the synthesis of type I collagen, and simultaneously reduce the abnormal expression of matrix metalloproteinase-9 (MMP-9) in tendon tissue, thereby improving the structure and function of tendons and tendon sheathing ( Chen et al., 2004 ; 2022 ; Auersperg and Trieb, 2020 ). Furthermore, clinical studies have shown that ESWT can significantly enhance patients’ grip strength, reduce the VAS pain score, and improve the Cooney wrist joint function score, confirming its effectiveness in alleviating symptoms and promoting functional recovery ( Asia Pacific, 2022 ). 4.2. Limitations Although this meta-analysis provides important evidence-based medical evidence for ESWT in the treatment of stenosing tenosynovitis, there are still certain limitations. Firstly, there is heterogeneity in the included studies. Different studies have differences in the selection of shock wave types (such as RSWT (Radial Shock Wave Therapy), FSWT (Focused Shock Wave Therapy), etc.), which may lead to different therapeutic effects. Moreover, the diversity of energy parameter Settings (such as energy density, impact times, frequency, etc.) makes it difficult to directly compare and summarize the research results. Furthermore, the control group Settings were also not the same. Some studies used placebo ESWT as the control, while others used drug treatment or other conservative treatment methods as the control, which increased the uncertainty of the results. Secondly, there is a significant lack of long-term follow-up data. Although this is sufficient to demonstrate the short-term efficacy and safety, no conclusion can be drawn regarding the long-term durability of the therapeutic effect after this period. The observed benefits may weaken over time, so re-treatment may be necessary. Due to the lack of long-term follow-up data, a comprehensive assessment of the long-term effect of ESWT cannot be made. Furthermore, there is a risk of publication bias. Since the publication of research results often tends to favor those with positive outcomes, there may be some unpublished negative studies, which may lead to the meta-analysis results overestimating the efficacy of ESWT. Furthermore, the included randomized controlled trial studies also have methodological flaws, such as unclear blinding procedures and unsecured allocation processes. In view of these limitations, the future research directions have clear goals. Firstly, multi-center, large-sample, double-blind randomized controlled trials (RCTS) should be carried out. Multicenter studies can include a broader patient population and reduce the limitations of the sample. A large sample size can improve the stability and reliability of the research results; Double-blind design can effectively reduce bias in the research process and improve the quality of research. By unifying the parameter Settings of ESWT (such as shock wave type, energy density, treatment frequency, etc.) and control protocols, better comparability is achieved among different studies, thereby providing more reliable evidence for the treatment of stenosing tenosheath with ESWT. Secondly, combined with imaging indicators such as ultrasound or MRI, explore the predictive factors of therapeutic effect. Ultrasound and MRI can clearly display the lesion conditions of the tendons, tendon sheaths and other tissue structures in patients with stenosing tenosynovitis, such as the thickness of the tendons, the amount of fluid accumulation in the tendon sheaths, and whether there is calcification, etc. By analyzing the relationship between these imaging indicators and the therapeutic effect of ESWT and seeking the factors that can predict the therapeutic effect, it is helpful to stratify patients before treatment, formulate more precise treatment plans for different patients, and improve the pertinence and effectiveness of treatment. 4.3. Future directions With the continuous deepening of research, the mechanism of ESWT in treating stenosing tenosynovitis will become clearer, and the treatment plan will be more precise and personalized. Combining imaging techniques to explore efficacy predictors and studying the combined application of ESWT with other therapies will further expand the application scope of ESWT in the treatment of stenosing tenosynovitis, improve the therapeutic effect, and bring more benefits to a large number of patients. It is believed that in the near future, ESWT will play a more significant role in the treatment of stenosing tenosynovitis, providing clinicians with more powerful therapeutic weapons and offering patients better medical services. 5. Conclusion In conclusion, the results of this meta-analysis indicate that ESWT is effective in relieving pain and improving function for patients with stenosing tenosynovitis, and it is also safe. However, the current research still has some shortcomings and requires further high-quality studies to be conducted for improvement. documents.title: The dual oncogenic and protective roles of hashimoto's thyroiditis in papillary thyroid carcinoma: a cohort-based meta-analysis.
documents.abstract: BACKGROUND: The clinical impact of Hashimoto’s thyroiditis (HT) in papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) remains controversial. HT has been implicated in multifocal tumorigenesis but also linked to more favorable tumor biology. This meta-analysis aimed to clarify their association. METHODS: This cohort-based meta-analysis followed PRISMA guidelines and was registered on PROSPERO (CRD420251138031). PubMed, EMBASE, Cochrane Library, and Web of Science were searched for studies comparing PTC patients with and without coexisting HT. Primary outcomes included multifocality, bilaterality, capsular invasion, vascular invasion, extrathyroidal extension, lymph node metastasis, distant metastasis, recurrence, and mortality. Secondary outcomes included BRAF V600E mutation and radioactive iodine therapy. Pooled odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated using fixed- or random-effects models. Subgroup, sensitivity, and meta-regression analyses were conducted. RESULTS: Forty-one studies involving 67,901 patients were included. HT was associated with increased risks of multifocality (OR = 1.13) and bilaterality (OR = 1.20), alongside reduced risks of extrathyroidal extension (OR = 0.85), capsular invasion (OR = 0.73), central lymph node metastasis (OR = 0.75), distant metastasis (OR = 0.33), and recurrence (OR = 0.74). No significant differences were found for vascular invasion, lateral lymph node involvement, mortality, or radioactive iodine use. HT was significantly associated with a reduced frequency of BRAF V600E mutation (OR = 0.55), especially in patients over 45. CONCLUSION: HT demonstrates a dual role in PTC, promoting multifocality while attenuating aggressiveness and adverse outcomes. Incorporating HT status into preoperative evaluation may enhance individualized risk stratification and guide surgical and adjuvant decision-making.

Background The clinical impact of Hashimoto’s thyroiditis (HT) in papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) remains controversial. HT has been implicated in multifocal tumorigenesis but also linked to more favorable tumor biology. This meta-analysis aimed to clarify their association. Methods This cohort-based meta-analysis followed PRISMA guidelines and was registered on PROSPERO (CRD420251138031). PubMed, EMBASE, Cochrane Library, and Web of Science were searched for studies comparing PTC patients with and without coexisting HT. Primary outcomes included multifocality, bilaterality, capsular invasion, vascular invasion, extrathyroidal extension, lymph node metastasis, distant metastasis, recurrence, and mortality. Secondary outcomes included BRAF V600E mutation and radioactive iodine therapy. Pooled odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated using fixed- or random-effects models. Subgroup, sensitivity, and meta-regression analyses were conducted. Results Forty-one studies involving 67,901 patients were included. HT was associated with increased risks of multifocality (OR = 1.13) and bilaterality (OR = 1.20), alongside reduced risks of extrathyroidal extension (OR = 0.85), capsular invasion (OR = 0.73), central lymph node metastasis (OR = 0.75), distant metastasis (OR = 0.33), and recurrence (OR = 0.74). No significant differences were found for vascular invasion, lateral lymph node involvement, mortality, or radioactive iodine use. HT was significantly associated with a reduced frequency of BRAF V600E mutation (OR = 0.55), especially in patients over 45. Conclusion HT demonstrates a dual role in PTC, promoting multifocality while attenuating aggressiveness and adverse outcomes. Incorporating HT status into preoperative evaluation may enhance individualized risk stratification and guide surgical and adjuvant decision-making. In 2022, more than 821,000 new cases were diagnosed worldwide, ranking it as the seventh most common cancer in terms of incidence [ 2 ]. Notably, the incidence in women is approximately three times higher than in men, while the disease-specific mortality remains relatively low, with an estimated 44,000 deaths reported in the same year. Papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC), which accounts for over 70% of all thyroid malignancies [ 3 ], is the most common histological subtype. Despite its increasing incidence, PTC typically exhibits indolent biological behavior, low mortality, and excellent long-term survival outcomes for the majority of patients [ 4 ]. Given this favorable prognosis, contemporary clinical management of PTC emphasizes long-term disease control and individualized treatment planning rather than short-term survival [ 5 ]. A key area of ongoing debate concerns the extent of thyroidectomy, whether total or lobar, particularly with respect to recurrence risk, postoperative complications, and the requirement for adjuvant therapy. Another central consideration is the use of postoperative thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) suppression. Although TSH suppression has been associated with reduced recurrence risk, prolonged therapy may adversely affect cardiovascular function, bone health, and overall quality of life [ 6 ]. These challenges highlight the need for more refined risk stratification models to support personalized therapeutic strategies in PTC. Hashimoto’s thyroiditis (HT) is the most common autoimmune thyroid disorder, and its prevalence has increased in parallel with that of thyroid cancer [ 7 ]. HT is characterized by extensive lymphocytic infiltration, the presence of thyroid-specific autoantibodies, and progressive glandular destruction. The coexistence of HT and PTC has been frequently reported, although its prevalence varies considerably among different populations [ 8 , 9 ]. The clinical significance of this coexistence remains a subject of ongoing debate. Some investigators propose that the chronic inflammatory microenvironment associated with HT may promote the development of PTC through mechanisms involving immune-mediated tissue damage and oncogenic signaling [ 9 ], Others argue that HT may be associated with less aggressive tumor behavior and improved prognosis [ 10 ]. In view of these divergent findings, it is essential to determine whether HT has a measurable influence on the clinicopathological characteristics and long-term outcomes of PTC. To address this, we performed a cohort-based meta-analysis of observational studies to systematically evaluate the impact of HT on tumor features, treatment approaches, and clinical prognosis in patients with PTC. Materials and methods This meta-analysis was conducted following the PRISMA guidelines, and where applicable, methodological recommendations from the MOOSE statement were also considered [ 11 ] (see Supplementary Table 1). The primary objective was to evaluate the clinicopathological characteristics, treatment strategies, and prognostic outcomes of patients with PTC coexisting with Hashimoto’s thyroiditis, in comparison to those without HT. In the absence of randomized controlled trials on this topic, only comparative cohort studies, including prospective, retrospective and matched cohort designs, were considered eligible for inclusion. A conventional pairwise meta-analytic approach was employed to evaluate differences between the HT and non-HT groups across a range of clinical endpoints. To account for interstudy variability and ensure the robustness of pooled estimates, a random effects model was applied. The study protocol was prospectively registered in the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO) to ensure methodological transparency and reduce the risk of bias (Registration No. CRD420251138031). Data sources and search strategy A comprehensive systematic search was conducted across four major electronic databases: PubMed, EMBASE, Cochrane Library, and Web of Science. The search strategy employed a combination of Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) and free-text keywords to ensure comprehensive coverage. Search terms included, but were not limited to: “Thyroid Neoplasms,” “Thyroid Carcinoma,” “Cancer of the Thyroid,” “Thyroid Cancers,” “Thyroid Adenoma,” “Papillary Thyroid Cancer,” “Papillary Thyroid Cancers,” “Papillary Thyroid Carcinomas,” “Hashimoto Disease,” “Hashimoto’s Disease,” “Chronic Lymphocytic Thyroiditis,” “Hashimoto Thyroiditides,” “Hashimoto’s Syndrome,” “Hashimoto’s Syndromes,” and “Hashimoto Struma.” The full search strategy is detailed in Supplementary Table 4. The search encompassed all publications from database inception through August 25, 2025. Both controlled vocabulary terms and free-text keywords were used in combination to enhance sensitivity and capture all relevant studies. Selection criteria Inclusion Criteria: Adult patients (≥18 years) with histologically confirmed PTC; Comparative cohort studies—including prospective, retrospective, or matched cohort analyses—assessing patients with coexisting Hashimoto’s thyroiditis versus those without; Patients undergoing initial thyroid surgery, with or without adjuvant therapy; Studies reporting at least one of the following outcomes: Primary outcomes were categorized into two groups: clinicopathological features and metastasis/recurrence-related characteristics. The former included multifocality, bilaterality, capsular invasion, vascular invasion, and extrathyroidal extension. The latter encompassed central lymph node metastasis (CLNM) and lateral lymph node metastasis (LLNM), which were analyzed as distinct endpoints, along with distant metastasis and disease recurrence. Secondary outcomes included BRAF V600E mutation status, treatment strategies (total thyroidectomy, radioactive iodine therapy), and all-cause or disease-specific mortality. Exclusion Criteria: Studies without a clear comparison between HT and non-HT groups; Studies with incomplete or non-extractable outcome data; Studies involving pediatric populations, patients with other autoimmune thyroid diseases (e.g., Graves’ disease), individuals with prior thyroid cancer treatment, or those with other concurrent malignancies; Studies without surgical intervention; Duplicate publications, case series, conference abstracts, or review articles. Study selection was initially performed through title and abstract screening. All included articles were independently reviewed in duplicate to ensure currency and eligibility. Disagreements were resolved by a third reviewer through discussion and consensus. Data extraction and quality assessment Data extraction was independently performed by three reviewers following the PRISMA guidelines. The extracted variables included: study characteristics (first author, year of publication, country, study design, and sample size); patient demographics (age and sex); tumor features (tumor stage, bilaterality, multifocality, capsular invasion, and extrathyroidal extension); treatment strategies (extent of thyroidectomy and use of radioactive iodine); and all eligible outcome indicators, along with their corresponding 95% confidence intervals (CIs) or raw event counts. The methodological quality of each included cohort study was assessed using the Newcastle–Ottawa Scale (NOS), which evaluates studies across three domains: selection (maximum 4 stars), comparability (maximum 2 stars), and outcomes (maximum 3 stars), for a total possible score of 9 stars. Studies were categorized as high quality if they received ≥ 6 stars, moderate quality if scoring 3–5 stars, and low quality if scoring < 3 stars. Studies rated as low quality were excluded from the final analysis. Discrepancies in data extraction or quality assessment were resolved through consensus-based group discussion. Statistical analysis Primary outcomes encompassed key clinicopathological characteristics—including multifocality, bilaterality, capsular invasion, vascular invasion, and extrathyroidal extension—as well as features related to metastasis and recurrence, such as CLNM and LLNM, distant metastasis, and disease recurrence. Secondary outcomes included BRAF V600E mutation status, treatment modalities (total thyroidectomy and radioactive iodine [RAI] therapy), and both all-cause and disease-specific mortality. Effect estimates were calculated as odds ratios (ORs) with corresponding 95% CIs to quantify the association between HT and each clinical endpoint in patients with PTC, in comparison with those without HT. All statistical analyses were performed using STATA version 16.0 (College Station, TX, USA). A conventional meta-analytic framework was employed, with pooled effect sizes computed using a random-effects model based on the DerSimonian–Laird method to account for between-study variability. Statistical heterogeneity was assessed using the I² statistic, with an I² value > 50% indicating substantial heterogeneity. Publication bias was evaluated by visual inspection of funnel plots and quantitatively assessed using Egger’s regression test, with statistical significance defined as α = 0.05. Given that only 24 of the 41 included studies were published after 2017—and with most reporting a mean patient age under 50 years (with only one exception)—a predefined subgroup analysis was conducted using 45 years as the cutoff, in accordance with the AJCC 7th edition staging criteria, to explore potential sources of heterogeneity [ 12 ]. A two-sided P -value < 0.05 was considered indicative of statistical significance throughout. Results Systematic review and characteristics of the included studies A total of 7,779 records were initially retrieved through the systematic database search. After the removal of duplicates and screening of titles and abstracts for relevance, 311 studies were selected for full-text evaluation. Upon review, 270 studies were excluded for the following reasons: incompatible research population ( n = 84), unavailable or incomplete outcome data ( n = 89), incompatible study design ( n = 50), and unrelated research directions ( n = 47). Consequently, 41 studies fulfilled the predefined inclusion criteria and were ultimately included in the meta-analysis (Fig. 1 ), comprising a pooled sample of 67,901 patients [ 13 – 53 ]. Among them, 17,516 patients were assigned to the HT group, while 50,385 patients constituted the non-HT cohort. A comprehensive summary of the study characteristics is provided in Table 1 . The results of the NOS quality evaluation are shown in Table 1 . The NOS scores of the included studies ranged from 6 to 9, indicating that all were high-quality literature. A fixed-effects model was employed due to moderate heterogeneity (I² = 44%, P = 0.08). The pooled analysis revealed a significantly higher incidence of bilateral disease in patients with coexisting HT (OR = 1.20, 95% CI: 1.12–1.29, P < 0.0001). Sensitivity analyses confirmed the robustness of this association (Fig. 2 A). With respect to multifocality, 36 studies contributed relevant data. Given the substantial heterogeneity across studies (I² = 75%, P < 0.001), a random-effects model was applied. The meta-analysis demonstrated a significantly increased risk of multifocal disease in the HT group compared to the non-HT group (OR = 1.13, 95% CI: 1.03–1.24, P = 0.01) (Fig. 2 B). To further examine the potential modifying effect of age, subgroup analyses were conducted using 45 years as the cutoff, in accordance with the AJCC 7th edition staging system. The positive association between HT and multifocality persisted across both age strata: OR = 1.16 (95% CI: 1.00–1.36) for patients aged ≤ 45 years, and OR = 1.17 (95% CI: 1.05–1.30) for those > 45 years (Fig. 3 ). Collectively, these findings indicate that the presence of HT is significantly associated with an increased likelihood of both multifocal and bilateral disease in PTC patients. This association may reflect a biological predisposition toward multicentric tumor development in the setting of autoimmune thyroiditis. ( A) Bilaterality; ( B ) Multifocality Fig. 3 Subgroup analysis of multifocality in PTC patients with and without coexisting HT Regarding aggressive pathological features, several findings indicate that HT may be associated with reduced tumor invasiveness in PTC. Ten studies reported on vascular invasion, revealing substantial heterogeneity (I² = 78%, P < 0.01). A random-effects model showed no statistically significant association between HT and vascular invasion (OR = 1.02, 95% CI: 0.82–1.26). Subgroup analyses stratified by age likewise showed no significant differences (≤ 45 years: OR = 1.58, 95% CI: 0.81–3.08; >45 years: OR = 0.90, 95% CI: 0.71–1.13). Four studies assessed capsular invasion. The initial pooled analysis showed no significant difference between groups (OR = 0.92, 95% CI: 0.50–1.70), with considerable heterogeneity (I² = 89%, P < 0.001). However, sensitivity analysis excluding the study by Feng Zhu et al. (2015) substantially reduced heterogeneity (I² = 15%, P = 0.31), and under a fixed-effects model, HT was significantly associated with a lower incidence of capsular invasion (OR = 0.73, 95% CI: 0.60–0.89). Thirteen studies evaluated extrathyroidal extension (ETE). Despite notable heterogeneity (I² = 75%, P < 0.01), the pooled estimate indicated a significantly lower risk of ETE in the HT group (OR = 0.85, 95% CI: 0.76–0.94). Subgroup analyses stratified by age confirmed this protective association across both age cohorts (≤ 45 years: OR = 0.83, 95% CI: 0.72–0.95; >45 years: OR = 0.84, 95% CI: 0.71–1.00). Taken together, these results suggest that HT is significantly associated with reduced risks of capsular invasion and extrathyroidal extension in PTC, while no meaningful association was observed for vascular invasion. ( A) capsular invasion; ( B ) extrathyroidal extension Metastatic and recurrence outcomes A total of 18 studies reported on overall lymph node metastasis (LNM) in patients with PTC. Due to substantial heterogeneity across studies (I² = 71%, P < 0.01), a random-effects model was employed. The pooled analysis revealed no statistically significant difference in overall LNM rates between patients with and without HT (OR = 0.91, 95% CI: 0.77–1.06) (Fig. 6 A). To further elucidate the regional impact of HT on lymph node involvement, subgroup analyses were performed for CLNM and LLNM (Fig. 6 B). Twenty studies indicated a significantly lower risk of CLNM in HT-positive patients (OR = 0.75, 95% CI: 0.66–0.86, I² = 77%, P < 0.001). In contrast, analysis of nine studies evaluating LLNM showed no significant difference between the HT and non-HT groups (OR = 0.89, 95% CI: 0.74–1.07, I²= 42%, P = 0.22). These findings suggest that HT is associated with a decreased likelihood of central, but not lateral, lymph node metastasis in PTC. Regarding distant metastasis, pooled data from eight studies demonstrated a significantly reduced risk among HT patients (OR = 0.33, 95% CI: 0.22–0.49), with negligible heterogeneity (I²= 3%). Eighteen studies evaluated recurrence, showing a trend toward lower recurrence rates in the HT group (OR = 0.74, 95% CI: 0.55–1.00), accompanied by moderate heterogeneity (I 2 = 60%). Four studies assessed disease-specific mortality, indicating a non-significant trend toward lower mortality in the HT group (OR = 0.47, 95% CI: 0.16–1.34), with low heterogeneity (I²= 0%). Collectively, these results suggest that HT may confer a protective effect in PTC, particularly by reducing the risks of distant metastasis and central lymph node involvement. The pooled analysis demonstrated a significantly lower mutation rate in patients with coexisting HT compared to those without HT (OR = 0.55, 95% CI: 0.45–0.67). Given the considerable heterogeneity among studies (I² = 72%, P < 0.001), a random-effects model was applied. Due to substantial heterogeneity across studies (I² = 75%, P = 0.007), a random-effects model was employed. The pooled analysis demonstrated no statistically significant difference in RAI utilization between patients with coexisting HT and those without (OR = 1.05, 95% CI: 0.75–1.47). Although the difference was not statistically significant, the overall trend indicated a lower frequency of RAI administration in the HT group, potentially reflecting a tendency toward treatment de-intensification in clinical practice. Sensitivity analyses confirmed the robustness of the findings, with effect estimates remaining stable upon sequential exclusion of individual studies. Subgroup analysis stratified by age revealed no significant difference in RAI usage among patients aged ≤ 45 years (OR = 0.85, 95% CI: 0.56–1.28). However, among patients > 45 years, RAI administration was significantly more common in the HT group (OR = 1.40, 95% CI: 1.20–1.63), with a statistically significant difference between subgroups ( P < 0.0001). These results suggest that while HT may not serve as an independent determinant for RAI therapy, its presence may influence clinical decision-making, potentially due to the typically indolent pathological features associated with HT-related PTC. Whether this observed trend reflects underlying biological distinctions or is primarily driven by treatment selection bias remains to be clarified through future prospective studies. See Fig. 9 . ( A) Overall RAI therapy; ( B ) Subgroup analysis stratified by age Meta-regression analysis To move beyond conventional pooled estimations and explore the underlying sources of heterogeneity, a multivariable meta-regression was performed, incorporating age, tumor size, follow-up duration, and extent of thyroidectomy as covariates. The analysis revealed that patient age ( P = 0.005) and tumor size ( P = 0.026) were significant contributors to the heterogeneity observed in the multifocality outcome. These results suggest that inter-study differences in baseline demographic characteristics and initial tumor burden may partially explain the variability in pooled estimates for multifocal disease. For extrathyroidal extension, follow-up duration was identified as a significant source of heterogeneity ( P = 0.047), indicating that discrepancies in surveillance periods among studies may have influenced the reported incidence of tumor extension beyond the thyroid capsule. None of the remaining covariates demonstrated a statistically significant effect on heterogeneity for other outcomes. Detailed results are presented in Fig. 10 . Discussion Principal findings This cohort-based meta-analysis demonstrates that HT is associated with a higher likelihood of tumor multifocality and bilaterality but with concurrently lower risks of several aggressive features and adverse outcomes, including extrathyroidal extension, capsular invasion, central lymph node metastasis, distant metastasis, and recurrence. The central novelty of this work lies in its comprehensive elucidation of this biological duality, by demonstrating a concurrent promotion of multifocal tumorigenesis and restraint of metastatic progression. Furthermore, our study provides robust, age-stratified evidence for the significant inverse association between HT and the BRAF V600E mutation, offering fresh insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying this clinical paradox. Implications The interpretation of certain outcomes, particularly the reduced incidence of CLNM, requires considerable nuance. The prevailing hypothesis of enhanced immune surveillance is critically challenged by a fundamental pathological confounder: the reactive lymphoid hyperplasia ubiquitous in the central neck of HT patients. This condition creates a significant diagnostic gray area, making the histological distinction between benign hyperplasia and true metastatic deposits exceptionally difficult [ 54 ]. Therefore, the reported lower CLNM rate may not solely reflect a biological protective effect but could substantially arise from systematic under-diagnosis, a profound form of pathological interpretation bias that future studies must address through standardized pathological protocols. This confounding likely explains the discrepant findings with prior meta-analyses, such as that of Liu et al. [ 55 ], and underscores that heterogeneity in surgical and pathological practices remains a major challenge in synthesizing this literature [ 56 ]. The observed associations with multifocality and bilaterality, while often attributed to a chronic inflammatory “field effect” [ 57 – 59 ], must likewise be contextualized within the reality of intensified diagnostic scrutiny. The persistent lymphocytic infiltration in HT creates a protumorigenic milieu through cytokines activating pathways like NF-κB and PI3K/Akt, fostering independent oncogenic events [ 60 ]. Yet, the constitutive ultrasonographic surveillance in HT patients inevitably increases the detection of small, subclinical multifocal foci, potentially conflating true tumorigenic potential with superior diagnostic capability [ 61 ]. The clinical implications of this “constrained” biology are direct and consequential. The predisposition to bilateral disease, coupled with the frequent pre-existence of subclinical hypothyroidism or the high risk of requiring lifelong hormone replacement even after lobectomy in HT patients [ 62 , 63 ], strengthens the argument for total thyroidectomy in appropriately selected patients, as the functional penalty of complete gland removal is often mitigated. Conversely, the indolent nature of the disease, corroborated by its favorable pathological and molecular profile, provides a strong rationale for considering conservative management strategies, including active surveillance, in low-risk cases [ 64 , 65 ]. This paradox extends to postoperative adjuvant therapy, where we observed no significant difference in RAI utilization overall, but substantial heterogeneity and age-dependent trends, reflecting persistent clinical uncertainty. Ultimately, preoperative knowledge of HT status, especially when integrated with molecular profiling, should inform a more personalized risk-assessment, guiding a nuanced balance between surgical intervention and treatment de-escalation [ 5 , 66 ]. Limitations This study has several limitations that should be considered. First, the findings are primarily based on pathological features and short-term outcomes; we did not evaluate long-term survival endpoints such as overall or progression-free survival, which limits direct assessment of HT’s influence on ultimate prognosis. Second, the predominantly retrospective design of the included studies carries inherent risks of selection and information bias. Third, despite identifying contributing factors through meta-regression, substantial heterogeneity remained unexplained for several outcomes. Furthermore, incomplete reporting of key parameters, including surgical extent, HT severity/duration, molecular classification, and antibody status—precluded more nuanced stratification and analysis. Finally, variations in geographic, ethnic, and clinical practices may affect the generalizability of our findings, particularly regarding BRAF mutation prevalence and treatment strategies. Future research must strive to disentangle this complex interplay by adopting standardized protocols for pathological assessment, molecular subtyping, and the reporting of HT-specific clinical parameters, including antibody status and functional thyroid data. Such efforts will be crucial in validating the model of “constrained carcinogenesis” and fully harnessing the prognostic and therapeutic implications of the unique immune-tumor interface in HT-associated PTC. Nonetheless, this meta-analysis integrates the most comprehensive body of evidence available to date and applies rigorous methodological standards to mitigate confounding influences. Collectively, the findings reinforce the complex dualistic role of Hashimoto’s thyroiditis in papillary thyroid carcinoma—both as a factor associated with increased tumor multiplicity and as a potential marker of favorable prognostic features.
